scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Calypso music has its roots in Trinidad in the 17th century from the West African Kaiso and Canboulay familiar to the enslaved Africans brought to the Caribbean islands to work on sugar plantations.
Modern calypso began in the 19th century as a fusion of disparate elements ranging from the masquerade song lavway, French Creole belair, and the calinda stick-fighting chantwell.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Calypso serves as a vital medium for sociopolitical commentary, news dissemination, and protest against authoritarian colonial culture.
Singers use the genre to lampoon politicians, critique economic inequalities, and voice community concerns during Carnival and national elections.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Calypso music is characterized by highly rhythmic and harmonic vocals, traditionally accompanied by steel drums (tambores metálicos) manufactured from recycled oil barrels.
Venezuelan variants utilize a rhythmic percussion battery based on the bumbac, charrasca, cencerro, and cuatro, while modern adaptations incorporate keyboards, electric basses, and horn sections.
Listen for the steel drums, bumbac, charrasca, cencerro.
The pulse is 2/4.
A syncopated 2/4 rhythm anchored by steel drums and percussive chatter, driven by witty, narrative-led vocal delivery and call-and-response structures.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Calypso performances historically center around seasonal 'calypso tents' and large-scale Carnival celebrations.
Performers and participants wear vibrant Carnival costumes, and competition winners traditionally join pageantry winners in the annual costume parade on Carnival Monday.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical and contemporary figures include Attila the Hun, Roaring Lion, Lord Invader, Lord Kitchener, Mighty Sparrow, Calypso Rose, and Harry Belafonte, who popularized the genre globally in the 1950s.
Regional expressions include benna in Antigua and Barbuda, spouge in Barbados, Dominica cadence-lypso, Venezuelan calipso de El Callao, Jamaican mento, and soca music.
Derived from West African Kaiso, French Creole belair, and calinda stick-fighting chants, calypso subsequently influenced international genres like ska and evolved directly into soca music.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Calypso is child of Soca: Soca emerged in the late 1970s from the blending of calypso with East Indian music, soul, and funk.
Calypso is sibling of Mento: Jamaican folk music style sharing roots and mid-century Caribbean popularity with calypso.

Form: verse-chorus with call-and-response. Mood: joyful, satirical, energetic.
